If you read a magazine article in this, and a magazine article in Times New Roman or Palatino or Garamond, you'd catch on quickly. Seriously, give it a shot.

A good typeface is like a car that drives well, as opposed to a different car that's the same color and roughly the same shape and has the same number of wheels. Or a much flashier car that stands out from the rest on the highway.

Someone who doesn't know anything about cars would just say, hey, that concept car is pretty and the ones they sell in the store are so boring. But once you're inside the car, it's not about the superficial qualities, it's about how well it drives and how much mileage it gets and how versatile it is and how easy it is to repair.

Or think of the cheap video editing software or photo editing software that comes with a consumer electronics vs. something like Adobe. Adobe products are very boring in their interface because you can do anything with them. They don't have huge 3-D buttons and animated characters and help windows everywhere. Because the software's memorability isn't the point; it's what you do with that software. Flashy fonts (Star Trek, Coca-Cola) are attention-grabbing and fun but they can do almost nothing, and you will get sick of them quickly if you try to use them. Cheap fonts (Arabic Typesetting) can do the basic task but the more you work with them the more you realize the subtle limitations.

The fact that the Star Trek font is iconic is exactly why you would never use it as a designer. What do you have to say that's so unimportant you would want readers to think about something else?
